content.title: About
content.content: Molasses is a thick, dark syrup obtained by boiling down the juice of sugar cane or sugar beet. It has a characteristic sweet‑bitter flavor, high mineral content, and less sucrose than regular sugar.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Molasses was used in ancient civilizations as an energy source and medicinal remedy.
There are several types: light (from beet), dark (from cane) and blackstrap (unrefined, mineral‑rich).
In the United States molasses is commonly added to baked goods, sauces, and barbecue marinades.
In the 19th century molasses was a major export commodity from the US to Europe.
Molasses contains iron, calcium, magnesium and potassium, making it popular among vegetarians.

items.title: Rich in minerals
items.content: Molasses provides iron, calcium, magnesium and potassium, which support blood, bone and muscle function.

items.title: Low glycemic index
items.content: Compared with regular sugar, molasses raises blood glucose more slowly, which can be beneficial when consumed in moderation.

items.title: Antioxidant properties
items.content: Phenolic compounds in molasses help combat free radicals.

items.title: Supports digestion
items.content: Fiber and natural enzymes in molasses aid normal gastrointestinal function.

items.title: Energy source
items.content: Glucose and fructose in molasses quickly supply the body with energy, making it popular among athletes.

items.title: High sugar content
items.content: Despite a lower glycemic index, molasses still contains a significant amount of sugar and should be consumed in moderation.

items.title: Cane allergy
items.content: Some individuals may experience allergic reactions to cane‑derived products.

items.title: Acidity
items.content: Molasses has an acidic pH, which can irritate the mucosa if consumed excessively.

items.title: Medication interactions
items.content: The high potassium level may affect the action of certain antihypertensive drugs.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Molasses is used in baking (cookies, bread, muffins), barbecue sauces, marinades, oatmeal and smoothies. It can be stirred into tea or coffee for a caramel‑like sweetness. For a milder taste, dilute it with water at a 1:1 ratio.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store molasses in a tightly sealed glass or plastic bottle in a cool, dark place. For longer storage keep it in the refrigerator to prevent crystallization and flavor changes. Discard if it develops a sour smell or off‑color.

pasta-whole-grain-with-tomato-based-sauc.title: Whole Grain Pasta with Tomato Sauce and Poultry

content.title: About
content.content: Whole grain pasta with tomato sauce and pieces of poultry is a restaurant menu item (3652). Whole grain pasta retains bran and germ, making it more nutritious than refined white pasta. The tomato sauce is made from ripe tomatoes, olive oil, garlic and basil, while chicken or turkey adds protein and aroma.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Whole grain pasta contains more fiber and micronutrients than regular refined pasta.
Tomatoes are rich in lycopene, which becomes more bioavailable after cooking.
The combination of carbs from pasta and protein from poultry provides lasting satiety.
Traditional Italian tomato sauce is simmered for 30–60 minutes to develop flavor.
Poultry is usually seared to a golden crust, preserving juiciness and adding savory notes.

items.title: High in fiber
items.content: Whole grain pasta provides soluble and insoluble fiber that supports digestive health.

items.title: Source of complex carbohydrates
items.content: The pasta delivers a steady release of glucose, offering sustained energy.

items.title: Lycopene from tomatoes
items.content: Lycopene is a powerful antioxidant that may reduce the risk of certain chronic diseases.

items.title: Protein from poultry
items.content: Chicken or turkey offers high‑quality protein essential for tissue repair.

items.title: Low in saturated fat
items.content: Prepared with a modest amount of olive oil, the dish remains heart‑friendly.

items.title: Gluten allergy
items.content: Whole grain pasta contains gluten, so individuals with celiac disease or gluten sensitivity should choose a gluten‑free alternative.

items.title: Sodium content
items.content: Tomato sauce can be salty; monitor added salt to keep sodium intake in check.

items.title: Foodborne bacteria
items.content: Poultry must be fully cooked to eliminate the risk of salmonella.

items.title: Caloric density
items.content: While balanced, portion size should be controlled to avoid excess calories.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Serve the pasta hot, tossed with tomato sauce and poultry pieces. Garnish with fresh basil, grated Parmesan, or a drizzle of olive oil for extra flavor. It pairs well with a light green salad.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store leftovers in an airtight container in the refrigerator for up to 2‑3 days. Reheat with a splash of water or broth to restore texture. Only the sauce can be frozen; keep pasta separate.

potato-french-fries-from-fresh-fried.title: Potato, French Fries, from fresh, fried

content.title: About
content.content: French fries are strips of fresh potato that are deep‑fried until golden and crisp. They have a crunchy exterior with a soft interior and a characteristic salty flavor. French fries are commonly served as a side dish or snack in fast‑food restaurants.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: The first recipe for fried potatoes appeared in 17th‑century Belgium.
In the United States French fries are considered a national dish, while in the Netherlands they are called "patat".
There are more than 30 cutting styles: classic sticks, crinkle‑cut, shoestring, waffle, and curly.
A double‑fry method (low temperature first, then high) is often used to achieve extra crispness.
In some countries fries are served with mayonnaise, ketchup, cheese sauce, or vinegar.

items.title: Rich in potassium
items.content: Potatoes provide potassium, which supports normal blood pressure and muscle function.

items.title: Vitamin C source
items.content: Freshly fried potatoes retain vitamin C, an antioxidant that protects cells.

items.title: Dietary fiber
items.content: Fiber in potatoes aids digestion and promotes a feeling of fullness.

items.title: Quick energy source
items.content: Starch converts rapidly to glucose, giving a fast boost of energy.

items.title: Contains iron
items.content: Potatoes contain modest amounts of iron, important for blood formation.

items.title: High calorie content
items.content: Deep‑frying adds many calories; portion size should be moderated.

items.title: Trans fats and saturated fats
items.content: Using old or overheated oil can create harmful trans fats.

items.title: Salt
items.content: Excessive salt intake may raise blood pressure.

items.title: Potato allergy
items.content: A small number of people may experience allergic reactions to potatoes.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Serve hot French fries with sauces such as ketchup, mayonnaise, cheese sauce, garlic aioli, or vinegar. Sprinkle with seasonings like paprika, rosemary, or garlic for extra flavor.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Cooked French fries are best eaten immediately. If needed, store in an airtight container in the refrigerator for up to 24 hours; reheat in the oven to restore crispness.

content.title: About
content.content: Rutabaga (also called swede or yellow turnip) is a root vegetable from the Brassicaceae family, cultivated in temperate climates. When cooked it becomes tender with a mildly sweet, nutty flavor. It is commonly used in soups, stews, casseroles, and as a side dish.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Rutabaga is rich in glucosinolates, compounds that may support the body’s detox pathways.
Compared with turnip, rutabaga has a lighter, yellowish flesh.
In Scotland a traditional dish is “Rutabaga soup” – a hearty broth with barley.
It can be stored in a cool place for up to six months.
In some regions it is known as “Swede” (Swedish cabbage).

items.title: High in vitamin C
items.content: Vitamin C supports the immune system and aids collagen synthesis.

items.title: Source of dietary fiber
items.content: Fiber promotes healthy digestion and helps maintain satiety.

items.title: Contains potassium
items.content: Potassium helps regulate fluid balance and supports heart function.

items.title: Low in fat
items.content: Rutabaga contains virtually no fat, making it suitable for low‑calorie diets.

items.title: Rich in antioxidants
items.content: Phenolic compounds protect cells from oxidative stress.

items.title: Allergy
items.content: A small number of people may experience an allergic reaction to cruciferous vegetables.

items.title: Gas and bloating
items.content: Large portions can cause gastrointestinal gas due to complex carbohydrates.

items.title: Thyroid interaction
items.content: Glucosinolates may affect thyroid function when consumed in very high amounts.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Boil or simmer until tender, add to soups, stews, casseroles, or mash into a puree. It can also be roasted with olive oil and herbs for a flavorful side.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store in a cool, dry place in paper or mesh bags. For longer storage keep in the refrigerator, where it stays fresh for up to six months.

white-beans-from-canned-no-added-fat.title: White Beans, Canned, No Added Fat

content.title: About
content.content: White beans, canned with no added fat, are a ready‑to‑eat product made from selected white bean varieties that are cooked until tender and packed in their own liquid without any added vegetable or animal fats. The beans retain most of their nutrients, and the lack of fat makes them a convenient low‑calorie option.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: White beans are also known as "navy beans", "cannellini" or "large white beans".
Canning without fat results in a lower calorie count compared with many other canned legumes.
Beans are a rich source of plant protein and are considered a good iron source for vegetarians.
Traditionally used in Mediterranean cuisine in soups, stews, and salads.
A sealed can can be stored for up to 3 years if the packaging remains intact.

items.title: Rich source of plant protein
items.content: One serving (about 130 g) provides roughly 7 g of protein, supporting muscle maintenance.

items.title: High in dietary fiber
items.content: Fiber aids digestion and promotes a feeling of fullness.

items.title: Low in fat
items.content: The absence of added fat makes this product suitable for calorie‑controlled diets.

items.title: Contains iron and magnesium
items.content: Iron contributes to hemoglobin formation, while magnesium supports muscle and nerve function.

items.title: Source of folate
items.content: Folate is essential for DNA synthesis and is especially important during pregnancy.

items.title: Legume allergy
items.content: Some individuals may experience allergic reactions to beans.

items.title: Sodium content
items.content: Canned foods often contain added salt; limit intake if you need to control sodium.

items.title: Gas formation
items.content: Legumes can cause bloating in sensitive people; rinsing before use can help.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Add the beans to salads, soups, stews, pasta dishes, or use them as a filling for vegetables. They are often rinsed with cold water before consumption to reduce sodium.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store unopened cans in a cool, dry place away from direct sunlight. After opening, transfer to an airtight container and keep refrigerated for no more than 3‑4 days.
